Control engineering · Thermal systems · Cadence PSpice

Modeling and Controlling a Thermal System with PID Compensation

From an oscillatory furnace model to a tuned PID controller and its analog circuit implementation.

This engineering laboratory focused on the temperature regulation of an experimental furnace monitored through a thermocouple. The objective was to study the system's transient and frequency responses, design a proportional–integral–derivative (PID) controller, and then implement that controller with an electronic circuit in Cadence/PSpice.

Engineering objective

Track a temperature setpoint accurately while reducing steady-state error, overshoot and settling time, without sacrificing stability.

1 VModeled setpoint step
4.5 sBest simulated 5% settling time
16 dBReported gain margin after tuning

Representing the furnace as a dynamic system

The furnace was represented by a fourth-order transfer function. The feedback loop compares the reference voltage with the modeled sensor output and drives the plant with their difference. The original study uses a 1 V step as the setpoint.

Plant transfer function
G(s) = 10 / [(1 + 0.1s)(1 + s)²(1 + 10s)]

The four poles capture the combined lag of the thermal process and its modeled dynamics. This transfer function is taken directly from the laboratory report; it is a simulation model, not an experimentally identified furnace.

Baseline behavior: oscillations and steady-state error

The initial closed-loop step response reached a reported maximum of 1.46 V for a 1 V reference and settled near 0.9 V. The measured overshoot was therefore 0.46 V, and the steady-state error was 0.1 V (10%). The oscillation period was approximately 8 s, corresponding to 0.125 Hz.

Performance indicators
ess = |Vref − Vout,ss|
Mp = Vpeak − Vref
fosc = 1 / Tosc

These indicators quantify accuracy, transient excursion and oscillation rate, respectively.

An open-loop AC sweep from 10 µHz to 100 Hz was then used to inspect the Bode magnitude and phase. The report identifies a small gain-margin magnitude of approximately 6 dB, supporting the decision to introduce compensation.

Designing a PID controller

The controller combines proportional, integral and derivative actions. The proportional term reacts to the current error; integral action addresses persistent error; derivative action influences transient damping.

Ideal parallel PID model
C(s) = Kp + Ki/s + Kds

Here Kp, Ki and Kd are the proportional, integral and derivative coefficients.

Initial tuning followed the Ziegler–Nichols ultimate-gain method. Setting integral and derivative gains to zero, the team tested proportional gains of 1.5, 2 and 3. A gain of 3 produced a divergent response, 1.5 a convergent response, and Ku = 2 sustained oscillations with period Tu = 6.33 s.

Classical Ziegler–Nichols PID rules
Kp = 0.6Ku
Ki = Kp / (0.5Tu)
Kd = 0.125TuKp

With Ku = 2 and Tu = 6.33 s, the initial coefficients are Kp = 1.2, Ki ≈ 0.38 and Kd ≈ 0.95.

The first complete PID simulation eliminated the reported steady-state error, but its 0.6 V overshoot exceeded that of the uncompensated system. The 5% settling time was approximately 11 s, motivating further tuning.

Improving settling time and overshoot

Keeping Kp = 1.2, the study varied Ki and Kd to compare transient performance. The following figures are reported in the original simulations.

KiKdOvershoot5% settling time
0.080.50.38 V10.5 s
0.120.70.35 V10 s
0.1610.30 V8 s
0.2030.15 V4.5 s
0.2550.24 V4.8 s

The selected gains provided the best reported compromise in this sweep: Kp = 1.2, Ki = 0.2, Kd = 3. A further increase in both Ki and Kd degraded the results, illustrating why larger controller gains are not automatically better.

Checking the frequency-domain robustness

The tuned system was evaluated again with a Bode analysis. The report records a 16 dB gain margin, a substantial improvement over the initial system and an encouraging robustness indicator for the simulated feedback loop.

Translating the controller into an analog circuit

The final part replaced the ideal PID block with a network of operational amplifiers, resistors and capacitors, implementing integral and derivative contributions electronically.

Component-to-gain relationships in the report
RdC = Kd
1 / (RiC) = Ki

The report gives C = 100 µF, with calculated resistances Rd = 9.5 kΩ and Ri = 26.3 kΩ. These resistance values correspond to the earlier nominal gains (Kd ≈ 0.95 and Ki ≈ 0.38), even though the surrounding text states that the optimized gains were used. This discrepancy is preserved here rather than silently resolved.

The simulated electronic implementation exhibited a near-zero steady-state error, an approximately 0.1 V overshoot and a 7 s response time. Its reported gain margin remained 16 dB.

Engineering takeaway

This project connects three essential engineering steps: modeling the plant, designing and tuning the feedback controller, and realizing the controller as an electronic circuit. The simulated ideal PID achieved the fastest reported response, while the analog implementation demonstrated how circuit choices and component values influence the practical behavior of a control system.

Key result

Within the modeled tuning sweep, PID compensation reduced the reported 5% settling time to 4.5 s, with a 0.15 V overshoot, negligible steady-state error and a 16 dB gain margin.

Original laboratory report: Rania CHETTAR · Anaïs SALLARD — ESIEE Paris, 2024–2025.
